newsitem.title: SPAIN: Mexican ex-prosecutor faces extradition from Spain.
newsitem.headline: Mexican ex-prosecutor faces extradition from Spain.

text.p: A fugitive Mexican former prosecutor wanted on charges of evidence-rigging and bodysnatching appeared in a Spanish court on Saturday to start a process that could lead to his extradition.
The former prosecutor, Pablo Chapa Bezanilla, was taken before Spain's special extradition judge, who ordered him held in custody until it could be determined if there was a case for extradition.
Chapa was arrested outside a Madrid restaurant on Friday after being on the run since February.
Spanish media reported that he denied all charges against him in a two-hour declaration and refused to return to Mexico voluntarily to stand trial.

Mexico, predicting a lengthy extradition battle, reacted immediately to Chapa's arrest by formally asking Spain late on Friday to begin steps return him, a spokesman for the Attorney General's Office in Mexico City told Reuters.

Chapa had just ended dinner a posh restaurant in the Spanish capital with his cousin Alberto Bezanilla and was leaving the restaurant when 20 national police agents, co-ordinated by Mexican police, surrounded him and told him he was under arrest, the spokesman said.
The former lawman put up no resistance and was taken away in a police vehicle, he added.
Chapa fled Mexico after authorities there accused him of evidence-rigging and bodysnatching while acting as special prosector in a case against the brother of former president Carlos Salinas.
The charges against him were filed on Feb. 8 after the discovery in late 1996 of the remains of a skeleton, including a skull, on the grounds of Raul Salinas' ranch on the outskirts of Mexico City.

Chapa had arrested the former president's brother in February 1995 on charges of masterminding the murder of Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu, secretary-general of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party.
The former lawman led the public to believe that the skeleton was that of a missing congressman who was wanted on charges of helping Raul Salinas execute the killing.
Special investigators and forensic experts, however, found that the body was that of a relative of a psychic who was helping Chapa with the investigation.
Mexican authorities allege that Chapa paid the psychic, known as "La Paca", to have a relative dug up from a cemetery and planted in Salinas' ranch.

Chapa was fired from his post in the Attorney General's Office last December. Once charges against him started to loom, he went into hiding. One report said he had requested political asylum in the United States.
Mexico's Attorney General Jorge Madrazo Cuellar, saying he was confident the country would win Chapa's extradition, counselled patience.
"The process will not be resolved in a few days and could well take months," Madrazo told Mexican television. Official predictions are for the process to last around six months.
Chapa also faces charges of possible illicit enrichment, giving false reports to official authorities and abuse of power.
